The agent explained that confirmed lost cards should be permanently closed rather than merely frozen, then verified her identity after she provided her full name and correctly confirmed DOB and email; verification was logged successfully at 2025-11-14 03:40 EST. Account lookup found three open checking accounts and no Rho-Bank credit cards. Debit-card lookups showed active cards on Light Blue, Green, and Light Green accounts. Transaction history showed no pending card purchases on Light Blue or Green, but Light Green had two pending card purchases ($75 and $127.45). The agent told the customer closure would have to wait for those transactions to settle, while a freeze could be applied in the meantime. After customer consent, tool responses confirmed Light Blue and Green cards were CLOSED for reason lost, and Light Green was FROZEN on 11/14/2025. The agent advised pending authorizations might still process and recurring payments on closed/frozen cards could be declined or need updating; the frozen card was to be permanently closed after pending activity settles.

Replacement follow-up: the agent reported Light Blue had hit its two-replacement rolling-year limit and a 48-hour post-closure wait; customer chose to wait rather than pay the stated $25 excess fee. A card-history response showed an older lost replacement issued 03/15/2025, and the agent estimated a slot might reopen on 03/15/2026. For Green, the customer selected expedited delivery and a free design; the order tool confirmed a CLASSIC replacement, $15 shipping charged, expected in 3–5 business days, pending activation on arrival. No replacement order was placed for Light Blue or Light Green. The last response said Light Green could remain frozen and the customer should contact the bank after pending transactions clear to close it and arrange replacement.

Observed limitation/outcome: the supplied evaluation feedback explicitly says success=false. Despite the user originally asking to replace all three cards, the exchange ended with only the Green replacement actually ordered; Light Blue was deferred and Light Green remained frozen pending settlement. There is no observed evidence that either deferred replacement was ordered or that the pending transactions later settled. The agent also could not establish a settlement timeline. Treat the account-specific actions and estimates as observations from this simulated conversation, not general bank-policy facts.

1. For account access/actions, verify identity with two accepted details and log verification before looking up or changing customer data. In this conversation the customer provided DOB and email; the verification log succeeded.
2. Retrieve all accounts, then all debit cards for each relevant checking account. Match card ownership/account and inspect current status before taking action.
3. Retrieve transaction history for each linked account and check for pending transactions. In this case, the two pending entries on Light Green were visible; the other two histories had no pending entries. Stop card closure for any card whose pending transactions remain, consistent with the retrieved closure procedure; do not infer an exact settlement date when none is established.

Explain pending authorized transactions may still process; revisit closure after settlement. The observation establishes the freeze succeeded, not how long settlement takes.

In this case, the Green replacement was explicitly approved with expedited shipping and free CLASSIC design; the order tool confirmed a $15 charge and 3–5 business-day estimate. Light Blue had a 48-hour post-closure wait and a possible $25 excess fee per retrieved tier guidance, so no order was made after the customer elected to wait.

The Green order confirmation explicitly returned order/card IDs, delivery estimate, and charge; the Light Blue age-out date was an agent estimate based on the listed issue date, not a later verified eligibility result.

No evidence establishes actual merchant settlement timing or completion of Light Blue/Light Green replacement orders.
